newsitem.title: USA: U.S. stocks end sharply lower on rate worries.
newsitem.headline: U.S. stocks end sharply lower on rate worries.

text.p: Renewed fears that the Federal Reserve will raise short term interest rates at its policy meeting next week sent U.S. stocks sharply lower Friday.

The interest rate jitters began to boil after news before the stock market opening that housing starts rose by a stronger-than-expected 2.6 percent in April. A selloff in shares of Hewlett-Packard Co also rattled investors.
The Dow industrials fell 139 points, or 1.89 percent, to 7195.
"We have a market that has come a very long way in a short period of time and it's vulnerable to some normal profit-taking," said Alfred Goldman, technical analyst at A.G. Edwards and Sons.
From its close at 6392 on April 11 to Thursday's record close at 7334, the Dow has climbed roughly 940 points.
Goldman said the stock market also had to contend with a "double witching" options expiration Friday.
Asked if a hike in short-term interest rates is possible at the Fed's open market committee meeting Tuesday, Goldman said, "my gut feeling is that they will."
But Goldman said after the rise that he anticipates in short term rates Tuesday, "the market will be negative for about half a day and that will be about it. It's still a bull market."

Jeffrey Applegate, chief investment strategist at Lehman Brothers, said stocks retreated Friday on the housing figures and a survey showing consumers in a more buoyant mood. In addition, he said a weak bond market and sell programs tied to the double expirations exacerbated the decline.
The 30-year Treasury bond fell 15/32, pushing the yield to 6.91 percent.
Applegate said stocks and bonds are locked in such a tight valuation range that it is all but impossible for stocks to go up whenever bonds make a substantial retreat.

Hugh Johnson, chief investment officer at First Albany Co, predicted the Fed would stand pat on Tuesday. He believes a slowing in the economy will persuade the Fed not to make a move. Although the housing starts were an exception, he said "the economic numbers for the second quarter have suggested fairly clearly that the economy is slowing."
As for the direction of the stock market, Johnson expects "a very sharp correction", which he said would be healthy.

Hewlett-Packard slumped 6-1/8 to 52-3/4. Late Thursday, the company reported second-quarter earnings of $0.75 per share, $0.05 below the consensus Wall Street estimate. While the earnings were up from a year ago, analyst Monika Eraiba of Gruntal & Co said the biggest problem in the latest quarter was a revenue shortfall.
Hewlett-Packard Friday announced an increase in the quarterly dividend to $0.14 per share from $0.12.
VeriFone Inc tumbled 6-1/2 to 51. Last month, VeriFone agreed to be acquired by Hewlett-Packard in a one-for-one stock exchange.

Trude Latimer, an independent analyst based in Charlottesville, Va., detected some strength in issues priced under $10 a share. She noted that Unisys Corp rose 1/4 to 6-5/8 and Northeast Utilities rose 1-1/8 to 9-5/8.
Declining stocks outpaced falling stocks by 1432 to 979 on the New York Stock Exchange.
The S&P 500 fell 12.13 to 829.75.
The Nasdaq closed down 12.85 at 1340.73.
Volume on the NYSE was 485.8 million shares.
((-- Wall Street Desk, 212-859-1881))
